channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: German investment in the US has fallen by around 80% against the period before Donald Trump's first term, the German Economic Institute says, with uncertainty over trade rules, tariffs and political intervention deterring large projects.
item.description:
The institute's reading is that the US remains an important location for its size, innovative strength and purchasing power, but that many companies are hesitant about new multi-billion projects, because uncertainty about future trade rules, possible new tariffs and political interventions complicates long-term investment decisions. The same report sets the corporate caution against a governmental counter-movement: Europe is broadening its economic relationships, with Canada now strongly in focus, and the EU and Canada are working on a comprehensive partnership intended to cover trade, security, supply chains, defence, space and research.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

An 80% fall describes a decision pattern rather than a market condition, and the reason given is not cost but predictability — the institute names uncertainty about future rules rather than any current tariff level. That distinction matters because a tariff can be modelled and priced into a project, while an unpredictable rule cannot, so the deterrent does not lift when a particular rate is settled. For a manufacturer weighing North American capacity, the practical consequence is that the hurdle is now partly about the variance of the outcome rather than its expected value. The parallel EU-Canada track is the alternative being built, though at government rather than company level so far. Points that may be worth considering include whether US capital projects are being assessed on a wider range of tariff scenarios than a year ago, and how a Canadian location would now be treated given both the US measures and the EU track.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: The Consultative Shipping Group, whose members carry more than a fifth of world trade by tonnage, says trade conflicts, wars and natural events are no longer temporary disruptions but a change in the framework of world trade.
item.description:
The group's members include Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Canada and Singapore. Der Standard's account gives one concrete measure of the change: more than 1,500 tankers are said to belong to the shadow fleet and to operate outside the usual rules. The reporting does not set out what the group is asking governments to do, or over what period the shadow fleet reached that size.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The distinction the group is drawing is a planning distinction rather than a diplomatic one. A disruption is something a supply chain absorbs with buffer stock and rerouting, on the expectation that the previous pattern returns; a change in framework conditions is something it has to be redesigned around, with different assumptions about insurance, transit time and route availability. A shadow fleet above 1,500 tankers is the most tangible evidence offered. The source does not say which rules those vessels operate outside; the reading here is that insurance and inspection cover are the exposures most likely to matter to a cargo owner. Points that may be worth considering include whether freight and insurance assumptions in the plan are built on a return to pre-war routing, and whether charter counterparties can be shown to sit inside the conventional regime.

Der Standard

item.title: Three Chinese ministries issued conduct guidelines telling carmakers to price on cost, stop frequent price changes and stop exporting vehicles unsuited to their target markets.
item.description:
The guidelines come from the Ministry of Commerce, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the State Administration for Market Regulation, and are reported by Nikkei Asia as targeting aggressive price cuts, frequent price changes and the export of vehicles that do not meet the needs of foreign markets. They call on automakers to set pricing strategies based on cost and guided by international supply and demand, and to refrain from disrupting market competition to gain unfair advantages; the code also warns against exporting products unsuited to the target market and usage environment, to stop brands simply offloading vehicles overseas. A separate package points the other way, at domestic demand: implementation opinions issued jointly by the commerce ministry, the market regulator and five other departments encourage local authorities to introduce car purchase support, to optimise purchase restrictions according to local conditions and to match replacement, additional-purchase and new-energy trade-in demand. The demand backdrop is an electrified one — a record 65.2% of the 1.54 million cars sold in China in August were pure electric or plug-in hybrid, above July's 65.1%, which the South China Morning Post links to fuel costs from the Iran war prompting buyers to shun petrol vehicles.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Read together the two measures describe an attempt to move Chinese vehicle output from price competition abroad to volume at home, and the second is the one that would change materials demand, on the reading that domestic purchase support and trade-in schemes would lift build rates rather than redirect finished vehicles. The export conduct rules matter differently: an instruction to stop exporting vehicles unsuited to their destination implies more market-specific engineering, which is where specification decisions get made. Cost-based pricing, if it takes hold, also reduces the pressure to strip cost out of the bill of materials, though enforcement is not described. Points that may be worth considering include whether Chinese vehicle programmes in the pipeline are export or domestic, and whether market-specific variants would change qualified content.

Herald Sun | China Economic Net | South China Morning Post

item.title: The All India Food Processors' Association has asked the Supreme Court to force a review of a proposed red hexagonal warning label for products exceeding limits in at least two of three categories: added sugar, salt or saturated fat.
item.description:
The association argues the thresholds require further scientific examination so that the framework rests on the most robust and internationally consistent footing available, and warns that many staples risk being covered in warnings that would tarnish the image of Indian food globally. The label was proposed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. The submission lands during what the reporting calls an unprecedented food safety crackdown in India, including nationwide raids on eateries over hygiene and standards. The reporting does not give a date for the labelling rules to take effect or say how the court has responded.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Warning-label schemes reach a materials supplier through pack redesign rather than through the rule itself, on this reading: a new graphic element with a defined colour and shape forces an artwork cycle, and that is the point at which substrate, ink and adhesive specifications may be reopened. The sources do not address any supplier consequence. The two-of-three threshold structure is also what makes reformulation a live alternative to relabelling, since a product can drop below the trigger rather than carry the mark. Which route manufacturers take determines whether the effect is a wave of artwork changes or a wave of recipe changes. Points that may be worth considering include whether Indian packaging customers have signalled a redesign timetable, and whether comparable schemes elsewhere offer a precedent for which route manufacturers take.

MarketScreener | Business Recorder

item.title: Federal, state and city money totalling EUR 400 million is going to Sanofi for a new Frankfurt insulin facility, built although the company says its existing plant is not profitable, so insulin stays available in the EU in a crisis.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung describes a practice of paying companies not to close factories so that they can go on producing goods that might one day be needed. Sanofi is building the Frankfurt insulin facility despite the existing plant being unprofitable on the company's own account. The report sets two comparisons alongside it: energy suppliers are already paid for reserve power stations that can step in during a dark lull even if they never generate, and similar thinking is being applied to the defence industry, which is to be compensated for keeping capacity free for drone production. The reporting does not say whether any similar mechanism is under consideration for chemical production.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reserve power station is the instructive comparison: the report notes suppliers are paid even if the plant never generates, which on this reading is a payment for availability rather than output, and the Sanofi case applies the same logic to manufacturing. If capacity payments extend from electricity and defence to pharmaceutical and then to other critical production, the question for a chemical producer becomes which of its outputs a government would classify as needed in a crisis, since that classification is what turns an unprofitable line into a funded one. It also changes how a closure decision looks: a plant that cannot earn its cost of capital commercially may still have a counterparty. Points that may be worth considering include which products in the portfolio would plausibly meet a crisis-supply definition, and whether the German resilience discussion has been engaged at association level.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Karl Kurz GmbH & Co. KG, behind the long-established cardboard manufacturer Tullau Pappen, has filed for insolvency, the Heilbronn district court has appointed a provisional administrator, and its 46 employees were told last week.
item.description:
The manufacturer is based in Rosengarten near Schwäbisch Hall, and the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung headlines its insolvency as coming after almost 150 years. The court appointed Tibor Braun of the Stuttgart firm IKB as provisional insolvency administrator, and he expects the provisional proceedings to run until the end of October. Employees' incomes are secured in the meantime by insolvency benefits from the Federal Employment Agency. The reporting does not give a cause, a turnover figure, or any indication of whether a buyer is being sought.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A 46-employee cardboard maker is not itself a supply event, and the interest is in what it indicates about the German board and packaging substrate base rather than in the company. Provisional proceedings running to late October set the date by which the outcome — continuation, sale or closure — becomes known, which is the point at which any customer of the plant would need an alternative qualified. The absence of a stated cause is worth noting rather than filled in: this report does not give one. Points that may be worth considering include whether any speciality board or laminate substrate is sourced from small single-site German converters, and what the qualification lead time would be for an equivalent substrate from another supplier.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The European Commission has proposed public procurement rules letting governments exclude bids that source more than half their supplies outside the EU, with no binding made-in-Europe quotas and an EU-wide tender platform.
item.description:
The proposal covers equipping schools, road construction and other public purchasing, and Bloomberg reports it extends to crucial public services including energy, water, railways, ports, airports and postal services. Public buying accounts for around 15% of EU output — about EUR 2.5 trillion in 2025 on MarketScreener's figure; Bloomberg puts the public contracts at stake at EUR 2.6 trillion. Two statements point to the reasoning behind the proposal: industry commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says many municipal authorities do not use opportunities that already exist to favour European companies, and Brussels officials are concerned public agencies believe existing rules oblige them to take the cheapest bid. The new rules are meant to clarify that authorities may prefer European suppliers over those from third countries such as China which do not grant European bidders equal access — but this is not to be mandatory, and unlike earlier plans for clean technology there are no binding made-in-Europe quotas. The package also creates an EU-wide platform intended to improve access and cut paperwork for bidders. MarketScreener places it in a sequence of single-market and supply-chain measures following warnings by Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta; Süddeutsche Zeitung frames the backdrop as an EU trade deficit with China of around EUR 1 billion a day.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The 50% threshold is the operative number. The proposal as reported grants buyers a discretion rather than imposing a duty on bidders, and says nothing about verification — but a threshold of this kind is only usable if origin can be evidenced, so the practical consequence on this reading is a documentation burden. If content were measured across the whole offer rather than at final assembly, which the reporting does not specify, the test would reach suppliers well behind the prime contractor. The optional character cuts both ways — it removes a compliance obligation but replaces it with unpredictability, because whether the criterion applies will vary by member state and by contracting authority. The sectors Bloomberg lists are infrastructure with long qualification cycles, where a materials specification set now persists for years. Points that may be worth considering include whether origin data exists at the granularity a content test would demand, and which parts of the portfolio ultimately reach a public buyer through a contractor rather than directly.

The Guardian | Bloomberg | MarketScreener | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Five Section 338 proclamations revise the scope of the Canadian tariffs from 15 September: cement and salt come out, all-terrain vehicles and further dairy go in, and import bans on alcohol, whey and molasses follow on 29 September.
item.description:
The proclamations were signed on 8 September according to China Daily, with the Globe and Mail dating the orders to 9 September, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and revise the scope of tariffs announced on 20 July. Products coming out of scope include rock salt and cement, with the Globe and Mail also listing toilet paper and fishing rods and exempting Canadian whiskey and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres; products going in include all-terrain vehicles and further dairy. The bans reach beer, wine, rye and vodka, whey protein, molasses, some dairy including cheese, and motorcycles. Two mechanical points carry beyond the product lists: the Painting & Coatings Industry trade press reports that the tariffs apply regardless of whether goods qualify as originating under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, and that they are imposed in addition to any applicable Section 232 tariffs. A Nanos Research poll cited by the Globe and Mail puts support for dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs in Canada at 80% of respondents who support or somewhat support them.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The two mechanical points matter more than the product lists, because they determine how a duty is calculated rather than what it lands on. Origin qualification under the trade agreement does not help here; and stacking on Section 232 means the rates are additive rather than alternative, so a landed-cost model that treats them as a single applicable duty will understate the charge. The scope revisions also establish that this list is being actively edited in both directions on short notice, which makes a one-off classification exercise insufficient. Points that may be worth considering include whether landed-cost models treat Section 338 and Section 232 as additive, and how quickly a classification review can be repeated when the scope is revised again.

Painting & Coatings Industry | China Daily | The Globe and Mail | The Globe and Mail

item.title: Germany's chemical employers' association and the IGBCE union are working at full speed on a joint plan for the sector's location and employment, after the government asked crisis-hit industries to propose measures.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that the federal government called on the collective bargaining parties in crisis-hit sectors such as chemicals to develop measures for growth, competitiveness and resilience, and that the Mining, Chemical and Energy Industrial Union and the Federal Employers' Association of the Chemical Industry have accepted the invitation. The reporting does not say what the plan will contain or when it is due. A parallel appeal has been made in Britain: the chief executives of SCI, the Chemical Industries Association, the Royal Society of Chemistry and the Institution of Chemical Engineers, among others, wrote to Prime Minister Andy Burnham asking the government to set out a clear vision for chemicals and a plan to deliver it with the sector. Their letter puts the UK chemical sciences at over GBP 60 billion of economic activity a year and around 140,000 direct employees, with supply chains contributing GBP 220 billion a year in gross value added and supporting 2.6 million jobs.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

What distinguishes the German process is that it runs through collective bargaining rather than through an industrial strategy document. The report does not say what the plan will contain, but on this reading an outcome reached between an employers' association and a union is more likely to reach labour cost, working time and site commitments than a government paper would, which would make it more consequential for a German site's cost base. The British letter is the conventional route by comparison, and the contrast is the point: two of Europe's larger chemical bases are working towards a sector plan, in one case at the government's prompting and in the other at industry's. Points that may be worth considering include whether German site planning assumes the current collective agreement framework holds unchanged, and which cost lines a location-and-employment pact would most plausibly reach.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | IChemE

item.title: Nan Pao Resins, Eternal Materials, Sheng-I Chemical and Everlight all reported higher August revenues, with Nan Pao up 14.2% and Sheng-I up 44.62% on a third consecutive monthly record.
item.description:
Nan Pao Resins Chemical reached TWD 2.221 billion in August and TWD 17.037 billion for the first eight months, up 11.4%, with both a record for the respective period. Sheng-I Chemical's TWD 1.385 billion was its third consecutive single-month record, taking the eight-month figure up 23.96% to TWD 9.373 billion. Eternal Materials rose 20.95% to TWD 4.07 billion in the month and 11.78% to TWD 30.331 billion for the eight months. Everlight Chemical Industrial's August revenue was TWD 747 million, up 33.2%, with the eight-month figure up 11.64% to TWD 5.705 billion. Pan-Well was the outlier on the month at TWD 134 million, up 1.12%, though its eight-month revenue rose 22.98% to TWD 1.105 billion. The report gives no cause for the increase.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is peer-group evidence rather than a market event, and the useful part is the divergence between the monthly and cumulative rates. Sheng-I at 44.62% for the month against 23.96% for the eight months, and Everlight at 33.2% against 11.64%, indicate demand accelerating within the year rather than a strong start being carried; Nan Pao's 14.2% against 11.4% is the steadier profile. Pan-Well is the counter-case, at 1.12% for the month against 22.98% for the eight months, which is the same pattern inverted. Because no cause is given and no end-market named, the figures establish that regional peers are growing without establishing where the growth sits. Points that may be worth considering include how comparable product line growth compares with these rates, and what would need to be true of end-markets for a spread this wide across five regional peers.

Commercial Times

item.title: Chinese brands took 8.7% of European new car registrations from January to July, up from 0.6% in 2021, and 11.7% of UK sales in eight months, where BYD and Jaecoo together now hold more share than Ford.
item.description:
The European figure comes from a Handelsblatt analysis of Dataforce data, which puts the share at almost three times its 2024 level and counts around 780,000 Chinese-brand cars newly registered in Europe in seven months — almost as many as in the whole of 2025. In Britain the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders puts the Chinese share at 11.7% for the first eight months against 3.8% a year earlier, with BYD at 3.5% from 1.9% and Jaecoo at 3.1% from 0.9%, selling 48,300 and 43,600 vehicles; over the same period Volkswagen fell to 8% from 9.1% and Ford to 5.4% from 5.9%. The movement in the other direction is visible in China itself, where August new car sales fell 49.9% for Honda, 51.9% for Nissan and 22.8% for Toyota, to 26,749, 28,275 and 118,400 units.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A share shift of this speed changes who specifies materials rather than how much material is needed, and the two questions have different answers. Incumbent European, US and Japanese brands losing share means volume moving to manufacturers whose supplier lists and qualification routes are, on this reading, different ones — and potentially whose engineering decisions are taken outside Europe. The sources give registration and sales data only and do not address supplier structures. The UK figures are the sharper version of the same trend and are worth watching as the leading indicator, since the share roughly tripled there in a year against a near-tripling over two years for Europe as a whole. What the data does not show is where these vehicles are assembled, which determines whether the materials demand follows the brand or stays in Europe. Points that may be worth considering include whether the automotive account plan is weighted to brands that are losing share, and what the qualification lead time would be with a Chinese manufacturer building in Europe.

Handelsblatt | China Economic Net | Bjd.com.cn | Commercial Times

item.title: Brent broke above USD 101 on 10 September, after Houthi attacks on four Saudi cities injured 73 people and Iran and the US struck ten ships and five tankers in the largest wave of attacks on shipping since the war began.
item.description:
The Houthi attacks on 8 September hit four cities and energy facilities in Saudi Arabia and forced some Saudi facilities to suspend operations. The same day the US destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, after accusing Tehran of firing ballistic missiles at a US warship twice in two days; Iran then said it had attacked ten ships near the Strait of Hormuz, and at least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed with another missing. The Independent sets the price against two earlier marks: Brent held at around USD 61 before the conflict and reached USD 138 in April when Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil passed in peacetime, before falling back during a prolonged ceasefire. Hong Kong Economic Times attributed the approach to USD 100 on 8 September to a double blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea route alongside the fighting in Yemen. Two second-order effects are already visible. Euro-area government bond yields rose in early trade as Brent touched USD 100, with investors also anticipating a quarter-point ECB increase, while the dollar index fell 0.2% to a near three-week low of 98.617. And in China, private refiners may cut run rates: crude imports fell below 30 million tonnes in June, the lowest since 2016, recovered to 37.9 million tonnes in August but remained about a quarter below a year earlier, and Energy Aspects puts their margins back at break-even from about USD 10 a barrel in early July.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The Chinese refining detail is the part most likely to be missed, because it points at demand rather than supply: if private refiners do cut runs as the report says they may, the effect on this reading would land in Asian product availability rather than in crude, though no source traces that consequence. For a buyer of hydrocarbon derivatives that means the petrochemical feedstock question is no longer only about crude price but about where barrels get processed. The Independent's USD 61 pre-war mark is the more useful anchor than the April USD 138 spike, since it defines how much of the current level is war premium rather than a new baseline. The bond-yield move also shows the cost channel widening from inputs into financing within the same session. Points that may be worth considering include whether feedstock contracts are indexed to crude or to product margins, and how much of the current price a plan should treat as reversible on a ceasefire.

Commercial Times | The Independent | Japan Today | Forbes Japan | Business Standard | Hong Kong Economic Times | MarketScreener | Lianhe Zaobao
